verses.zh: 我们岂是又举荐自己吗？岂像别人用人的荐信给你们或用你们的荐信给人吗？
verses.en: Are we beginning to commend ourselves again? We don’t need letters of recommendation to you or from you as some other people do, do we?[NOTE:1]
notes: The Greek construction anticipates a negative reply (“No, we do not”) which is indicated in the translation by the ‘tag’ at the end, “do we?”

verses.zh: 你们就是我们的荐信，写在我们的心里，被众人所知道所念诵的。
verses.en: You yourselves are our letter,[NOTE:1] written on our hearts, known and read by everyone,
notes: That is, “letter of recommendation.”

verses.zh: 你们明显是基督的信，藉着我们修成的。不是用墨写的，乃是用永生　神的灵写的；不是写在石版上，乃是写在心版上。
verses.en: revealing[NOTE:1] that you are a letter of Christ, delivered by us,[NOTE:2] written not with ink but by the Spirit of the living God, not on stone tablets[NOTE:3] but on tablets of human hearts.
notes: Or “making plain.”

Grk “cared for by us,” an expression that could refer either to the writing or the delivery of the letter (BDAG 229 s.v. διακονέω 1). Since the following phrase refers to the writing of the letter, and since the previous verse speaks of this “letter” being “written on our [Paul’s and his companions’] hearts” it is more probable that the phrase “cared for by us” refers to the delivery of the letter (in the person of Paul and his companions).
An allusion to Exod 24:12; 31:18; 34:1; Deut 9:10-11.

verses.zh: 我们因基督，所以在　神面前才有这样的信心。
verses.en: Now we have such confidence in God through Christ.

verses.zh: 并不是我们凭自己能承担甚么事；我们所能承担的，乃是出于　神。
verses.en: Not that we are adequate[NOTE:1] in ourselves to consider anything as if it were coming from ourselves, but our adequacy[NOTE:2] is from God,
notes: Or “competent.”
Or “competence.”

verses.zh: 他叫我们能承当这新约的执事，不是凭着字句，乃是凭着精意；因为那字句是叫人死，精意（或译：圣灵）是叫人活。
verses.en: who made us adequate[NOTE:1] to be servants of a new covenant[NOTE:2] not based on the letter but on the Spirit, for the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.
notes: Or “competent.”
This new covenant is promised in Jer 31:31-34; 32:40.

verses.zh: 那用字刻在石头上属死的职事尚且有荣光，甚至以色列人因摩西面上的荣光，不能定睛看他的脸；这荣光原是渐渐退去的，
verses.en: But if the ministry that produced death—carved in letters on stone tablets[NOTE:1]—came with glory, so that the Israelites[NOTE:2] could not keep their eyes fixed on the face of Moses because of the glory of his face[NOTE:3] (a glory[NOTE:4] which was made ineffective),[NOTE:5]
notes: Grk “on stones,” but since this is clearly an allusion to the tablets of the Decalogue (see 2 Cor 3:3) the word “tablets” was supplied in the translation to make the connection clear.
Grk “so that the sons of Israel.”
The glory of his face. When Moses came down from Mt. Sinai with the tablets of the Decalogue, the people were afraid to approach him because his face was so radiant (Exod 34:29-30).
The words “a glory” are not in the Greek text, but the reference to “glory” has been repeated from the previous clause for clarity.

Or “which was transitory.” Traditionally this phrase is translated as “which was fading away.” The verb καταργέω in the corpus Paulinum uniformly has the meaning “to render inoperative, ineffective”; the same nuance is appropriate here. The glory of Moses’ face was rendered ineffective by the veil Moses wore. For discussion of the meaning of this verb in this context, see S. J. Hafemann, Paul, Moses, and the History of Israel (WUNT 81), 301-13. A similar translation has been adopted in the two other occurrences of the verb in this paragraph in vv. 11 and 13.

verses.zh: 何况那属灵的职事岂不更有荣光吗？
verses.en: how much more glorious will the ministry of the Spirit be?[NOTE:1]
notes: Grk “how will not rather the ministry of the Spirit be with glory?”

verses.zh: 若是定罪的职事有荣光，那称义的职事荣光就越发大了。
verses.en: For if there was glory in the ministry that produced condemnation,[NOTE:1] how much more does the ministry that produces righteousness[NOTE:2] excel[NOTE:3] in glory!
notes: Grk “the ministry of condemnation”; translated as an objective genitive, “the ministry that produced condemnation.”
Grk “the ministry of righteousness”; translated as an objective genitive, “the ministry that produces righteousness.”
Traditionally, “abound.”

verses.zh: 那从前有荣光的，因这极大的荣光就算不得有荣光了；
verses.en: For indeed, what had been glorious now[NOTE:1] has no glory because of the tremendously greater glory of what replaced it.[NOTE:2]
notes: Grk “in this case.”
The words “of what replaced it” are not in the Greek text, but have been supplied to clarify the meaning.

verses.zh: 若那废掉的有荣光，这长存的就更有荣光了。
verses.en: For if what was made ineffective[NOTE:1] came with[NOTE:2] glory, how much more has what remains[NOTE:3] come in glory!
notes: Or “what was fading away.” See note on “which was made ineffective” in v. 7.
Or “through” (διά, dia).
Or “what is permanent.”

verses.zh: 我们既有这样的盼望，就大胆讲说，
verses.en: Therefore, since we have such a hope, we behave with great boldness,[NOTE:1]
notes: Or “we employ great openness of speech.”

verses.zh: 不像摩西将帕子蒙在脸上，叫以色列人不能定睛看到那将废者的结局。
verses.en: and not like Moses who used to put a veil over his face to keep the Israelites[NOTE:1] from staring[NOTE:2] at the result[NOTE:3] of the glory that was made ineffective.[NOTE:4]
notes: Grk “the sons of Israel.”
Or “from gazing intently.”

Or “end.” The word τέλος (telos) can mean both “a point of time marking the end of a duration, end, termination, cessation” and “the goal toward which a movement is being directed, end, goal, outcome” (see BDAG 998-999 s.v.). The translation accepts the interpretation that Moses covered the glory of his face with the veil to prevent Israel from being judged by the glory of God (see S. J. Hafemann, Paul, Moses, and the History of Israel [WUNT 81], 347-62); in this case the latter meaning for τέλος is more appropriate.
Or “was fading away”; Grk “on the result of what was made ineffective.” The referent (glory) has been specified in the translation for clarity. See note on “which was made ineffective” in v. 7.

verses.zh: 但他们的心地刚硬，直到今日诵读旧约的时候，这帕子还没有揭去。这帕子在基督里已经废去了。
verses.en: But their minds were closed.[NOTE:1] For to this very day, the same veil remains when they hear the old covenant read.[NOTE:2] It has not been removed because only in Christ is it taken away.[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “their minds were hardened.”

Grk “the same veil remains at the reading of the old covenant”; the phrase “they hear” has been introduced (“when they hear the old covenant read”) to make the link with the “Israelites” (v. 13) whose minds were closed (v. 14a) more obvious to the reader.
Or “only in Christ is it eliminated.”

verses.zh: 然而直到今日，每逢诵读摩西书的时候，帕子还在他们心上。
verses.en: But until this very day whenever Moses is read, a veil lies over their minds,[NOTE:1]
notes: Grk “their heart.”

verses.zh: 但他们的心几时归向主，帕子就几时除去了。
verses.en: but when one[NOTE:1] turns to the Lord, the veil is removed.[NOTE:2]
notes: Or perhaps “when(ever) he turns,” referring to Moses.
An allusion to Exod 34:34. The entire verse may refer to Moses, viewing him as a type portraying the Jewish convert to Christianity in Paul’s day.

verses.zh: 主就是那灵；主的灵在哪里，那里就得以自由。
verses.en: Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is present,[NOTE:1] there is freedom.
notes: Grk “where the Spirit of the Lord is”; the word “present” is supplied to specify that the presence of the Lord’s Spirit is emphasized rather than the mere existence of the Lord’s Spirit.

verses.zh: 我们众人既然敞着脸得以看见主的荣光，好像从镜子里返照，就变成主的形状，荣上加荣，如同从主的灵变成的。
verses.en: And we all, with unveiled faces reflecting the glory of the Lord,[NOTE:1] are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another,[NOTE:2] which is from[NOTE:3] the Lord, who is the Spirit.[NOTE:4]
notes: Or “we all with unveiled faces beholding the glory of the Lord as in a mirror.”
Grk “from glory to glory.”
Grk “just as from.”
Grk “from the Lord, the Spirit”; the genitive πνεύματος (pneumatos) has been translated as a genitive of apposition.

READING CYCLE THREE (see
"Bible
Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which
means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the
light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not
relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare
your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is
the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every
paragraph has one and only one subject.

- First paragraph

- Second paragraph

- Third paragraph, etc.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

- The emphasis of this chapter is very similar to the emphasis of the Book of Hebrews. It is a comparison
between the Old Covenant and the New Covenant (see Hard Sayings of the Bible, pp. 619-621). How are
sinful humans made right with God?

For a good discussion of these two covenants, see Dale Moody, The Word of Truth, pp. 52-57.

- performance of the Mosaic Law

- faith in the atoning work of God in Christ?

This comparison is used by Paul to defend his gospel and himself against the Jewish-oriented
false teachers who have arrived in Corinth from Palestine.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE SUPERIORITY OF THE NEW COVENANT OVER THE MOSAIC COVENANT

- This chapter's use of the term "spirit" is highly ambiguous. There has been much discussion over
2 Cor. 3:6,8,17, and 18. Are they relating to

- the "Holy Spirit"

- the concept of "the spiritual"

- There seems to be an intentional fluidity between the two.

The new age is the age of the Spirit (cf. Jer. 31:31-34; Ezek. 36:22-36), which inaugurates a
spiritual relationship with God versus a legal, performance-based relationship (2 Cor. 3:6).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SPIRIT IN THE NT

- Paul's use of the term "law" (see
SPECIAL TOPIC: PAUL'S VIEWS OF THE MOSAIC LAW)

- law = wrath; Rom. 3:20; 4:15; Gal. 2:16; 3:10-13; Col. 2:14

- law = spiritually good; Rom. 7:12-14,16; 1 Tim. 1:8

- contrast between Rom. 2:13; 8:6-7; Gal. 3:11-12,21-22; 2 Cor. 3:6-11

- Paul uses Abraham and Moses as two typological symbols of the relationship between "faith" and "law"; Gal. 4:21-31

The Law is good. It is from God. It served, and continues to serve, a divine purpose (cf. Matt. 5:17-19;
Rom. 7:7,12,14,22,25). It can not bring peace or salvation. James Stewart in his book A Man in Christ,
shows Paul's paradoxical thinking and writing:

"You would naturally expect a man who was setting himself to construct a system of thought
and doctrine to fix as rigidly as possible the meanings of the terms he employed. You would expect him
to aim at precision in the phraseology of his leading ideas. You would demand that a word, once used by
your writer in a particular sense should bear that sense throughout. But to look for this from Paul is to
be disappointed. Much of his phraseology is fluid, not rigid. . .'The law is holy,' he writes, 'I delight in the
law of God after the inward man' (cf. Rom. 7:12-13) but it is clearly another aspect of nomos that
makes him say elsewhere, 'Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law' (cf. Gal. 3:13)" (p. 26).

- Paul uses three major images in this chapter:

- letters, 2 Cor. 3:1-3

- letters of recommendation, 2 Cor. 3:1

- they are letters, 2 Cor. 3:2

- OT tablets, 2 Cor. 3:3

- Old and New Covenants, 2 Cor. 3:6-11

- written versus spiritual, 2 Cor. 3:3,6

- kills versus gives life, 2 Cor. 3:6

- veil, 2 Cor. 3:7, 12-16

- Moses, 2 Cor. 3:12

- Jews of Paul's day, 2 Cor. 3:14

- believers, 2 Cor. 3:14-16

SPECIAL TOPIC: LETTERS OF RECOMMENDATION

SPECIAL TOPIC: VEIL, SHAWL, COVERING

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: 2 CORINTHIANS 3:1-3

1Are we beginning to commend ourselves again? Or do we need, as some, letters
of commendation to you or from you? 2You are our letter, written in our hearts, known and read by all men; 3being manifested
that you are a letter of Christ, cared for by us, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts.

3:1 The grammatical form of both questions in 2 Cor. 3:1 expects a "no" answer. It is hard to know if Paul
is being sarcastic or heart broken.

▣ "to commend" This word is a compound of "to place" and "together," which is used as imagery

- to demonstrate (cf. Rom. 3:5; 5:8; 2 Cor. 7:11; Gal. 2:18)

- to endure (cf. Col. 1:17)

- to commend (cf. Rom. 16:1; 2 Cor. 3:1; 4:2; 5:12; 6:4; 10:12,18; 12:11)

▣ "as some" Paul uses this designation often in 2 Corinthians because of the conflict with the aggressive
false teachers from Palestine who tried to elevate themselves by contrasting themselves to Paul and his
background and his gospel (cf. 2 Cor. 3:2; 2:17; 10:2). Paul also used the same expression in a negative sense
in 1 Corinthians to relate to the actions and beliefs of some church members (cf. 2 Cor. 4:18; 15:12).

▣ "letters of commendation" The early church adopted the procedure of letters of recommendation to
assure the orthodoxy and trustworthiness of itinerant ministers.

- delegation from Jerusalem to Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia ‒ Acts 15:22,25-27

- Paul ‒ Acts 18:27

- Phoeba ‒ Rom. 16:1

- Timothy ‒ 1 Cor. 16:10-11; Phil. 2:19-24

- the household of Stephanas ‒ 1 Cor. 16:15-18

- persons taking the collection from the Gentile churches to the mother church in Jerusalem ‒ 2 Cor. 8:16-24

- Tychicus ‒ Eph. 6:21-22

- Epaphroditus ‒ Phil 2:25-29

- Philemon ‒ the book of Philemon

- Demetrius ‒ 3 John v. 12

SPECIAL TOPIC: LETTERS OF RECOMMENDATION

3:2 "You are our letter, written in our hearts," Paul is asserting that he does not need a letter to recommend
himself to this church (or from this church), because he is its spiritual founder as Christ is its savior and Lord.
They were his flesh-and-blood letter (cf. 2 Cor. 3:3).

The phrase "written in our hearts" is a PERFECT PASSIVE PARTICIPLE. Paul loved this church.
They were permanently in his heart and mind. The PASSIVE VOICE implies that God/Christ/Spirit is the agent
(cf. 2 Cor. 3:3), which produces Paul's love.

The idea of something being written on the heart (not in a letter) seems to be borrowed from the terminology
of the New Covenant in Jer. 31:33. It denotes an internal motive for one's actions inspired by the Spirit.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE HEART

▣ "known and read" There is a sound play between these two Greek words
(i.e., ginōskomenē and anaginōskomenē, cf. 2 Cor. 1:13). Both
are PRESENT PASSIVE PARTICIPLES.

▣ "by all men" This is the use of the term "all" where it is not inclusive (cf. Rom. 11:26). This is
obviously a hyperbole, so common in Jewish literature (cf. Matt. 5:29-30,38-42; 6:24; 7:3-5; 23:23-24).

SPECIAL TOPIC: EASTERN LITERATURE

3:3 "being manifested" See note at 2 Cor. 2:14.

▣ "you are a letter of Christ" Believers are meant to clearly reveal Christ by their motives, words,
and actions. How we live reflects on His reputation!

▣ "cared for by us" See
SPECIAL TOPIC: SERVANT LEADERSHIP

▣ "the Spirit of the living God" The terminology referring to the Triune God (see
SPECIAL TOPIC: THE TRINITY) is very fluid. The Spirit is often referred to as the Spirit of Jesus (cf. Rom. 8:9;
2 Cor. 3:17; Gal. 4:6; 1 Pet. 1:11; see
SPECIAL TOPIC: JESUS AND THE SPIRIT). Here the same type of fluidity is directed toward the Father.

The title "living God" is a play on YHWH, which is from the Hebrew VERB "to be"
(cf. Exod. 3:14; see SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.).
The descriptive title is common for the Father in the NT (cf. Matt. 16:16; 26:63; Acts 14:15;
Rom. 9:26; 2 Cor. 6:16; 1 Thess. 1:9; 1 Tim. 3:15; 4:10; Heb. 3:12; 9:14; 10:31; 12:22; Rev. 7:2;
see SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FATHERHOOD OF GOD).
In the OT the pagan idols were lifeless. They could not respond or they were dead part of the year
(i.e., the winter) following the fertility cycles of nature. YHWH was the only truly alive,
always-alive God!

▣ "not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts" This seems to relate to the giving of the law in
Exod. 31:18 and to the promise of a New Covenant (cf. Jer. 31:31-34 and Ezek. 36:22-36). This is an obvious contrast
between the Old Covenant as external law versus the New Covenant as internal (i.e., new heart, new mind, and new spirit,
cf. Ezek. 11:19; 36:26).

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: 2 CORINTHIANS 3:4-6

4Such confidence we have through Christ toward God. 5Not that we are adequate in ourselves to consider anything as coming
from ourselves, but our adequacy is from God, 6who also made us adequate as servants of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the
Spirit; for the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.

3:4 "confidence" This is another Pauline term used mostly in 2 Corinthians . It comes from the same Greek
root as faith, trust, believe (i.e., peithō and pistis, pisteuō). It basically means trust,
confidence, or reliance.

- positive context:

- Paul's travel plans, 2 Cor. 1:15

- Paul's confidence in God through Christ, 2 Cor. 3:4

- Paul's confidence in Titus, 2 Cor. 8:22

- Paul's confidence in Christ, Eph. 3:12

- negative context:

- Paul wants to be gentle with them, 2 Cor. 10:2

- Paul's reluctant comparison of his credentials with the false teachers, Phil. 3:4

3:5 "Not that we are adequate in ourselves" The Greek term hikanos is common in the NT and is used in two senses.

- as a large number of something (cf. 2 Cor. 11:30), even time

- fit, appropriate (cf. 2 Cor. 2:16), competent, qualified, able, or adequate

The second sense is used here. Paul expresses his sense of unworthiness using this term in 1 Cor. 15:9.
He also asserts that gospel ministers are not worthy in themselves in 2 Cor. 2:16 and 3:5.

Yet, even as we are inadequate in ourselves, God has called us and empowered us as His
representatives (cf. 2 Cor. 3:6). We are adequate in Him (cf. Col. 1:12).

▣ "to consider" This is the term logizomai, which is used thirty-four times by Paul, but
less than seven in the rest of the NT (cf. 2 Cor. 3:5; 5:19; 10:2,7; 11:5; 12:6). It reflects Paul's logical
presentation of truths and then as encouragement to think through the issues clearly.

The term is a major theological word because of:

- its use in the Septuagint for personalized truth (cf. the New International Dictionary of NT Theology, vol. 3, p. 823)

- its use in Gen. 15:6, which Paul uses to justify OT righteousness based on a free gift of God through faith (cf. Rom. 4:3)

- it may have been a technical term used by Sophists in their rhetorical presentations (see Bruce W. Winter, Philo and
Paul Among the Sophists)

Modern believers should also carefully consider what they believe about the faith and why. Our
mental and verbal abilities are part of the image of God in mankind. We must worship God with our minds
(cf. LXX Deut. 6:5; Matt. 22:37). We need to be able to give an account of the hope that is in us (cf. 1 Pet. 3:15).
We must think through our faith beliefs for our own stability and for evangelism.

SPECIAL TOPIC: A TRUSTWORTHY OT

SPECIAL TOPIC: A TRUSTWORTHY NT

SPECIAL TOPIC: IS CHRISTIANITY TRUE?

3:6 "servants of a new covenant" Wow, wow! Surprising to Jewish people, a "new" covenant (cf. Jer. 31:31-34;
Ezek. 36:22-36). Jesus used this terminology at the Last Supper (i.e., Matt. 26:28; Mark 14:24; Luke 22:20)

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

▣ "not of the letter but of the Spirit" There is a series of comparisons.

- written versus spiritual, 2 Cor. 3:3 and 6

- letter versus Spirit, 2 Cor. 3:6

- old service versus spiritual service, 2 Cor. 3:7

- the service connected with condemnation versus the service connected with right-standing, 2 Cor. 3:9

- what has passed away versus what is permanent, 2 Cor. 3:11

- the veil remains unlifted versus the veil is removed, 2 Cor. 3:14

Paul is contrasting the old and new covenants, but really heart faith (cf. Rom. 2:29; 7:6)
versus head faith (i.e., tradition, legalism, human performance, self-righteousness).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE SUPERIORITY OF THE NEW COVENANT OVER THE MOSAIC COVENANT

▣ "the letter kills" This seems to relate to the primary purpose of the Mosaic law. It was given
not to give life, but to accentuate and reveal our sinfulness (cf. Rom. 7:9-11; Gal. 3).

The Law brings

- condemnation (cf. Rom. 5:13; Gal. 3:10)

- wrath (cf. Rom. 4:15)

- death (cf. Rom. 7:11; 2 Cor. 3:7)

- see George E. Ladd's A Theology of the New Testament, pp. 495-510). The place of the law is also clearly seen in
Rom. 3:20; 5:20; 10:4; Gal. 3:23-29.

The relationship between the NT believer and the OT Law has been a
greatly confused issue. It seems to me, based on all the passages of the NT, that the Christian is not
under OT law (cf. Acts 15:7-11; Rom. 6:14; Gal. 5:18). This is not because the OT law has passed away (i.e., Matt. 5:17-19),
but because the NT Christian fulfills the OT law in God's love relationships with us seen in believers' love for others
(cf. Rom. 13:8-10; 1 Cor. 13; Gal. 5:14; 1 John 4).

The purpose of the law is to bring fallen mankind to Christ, so as to redeem
them. However, just because the OT law is not a means of salvation does not mean it is not God's will for
humanity in society (cf. Matt. 5:17-19; Rom. 8:4).

SPECIAL TOPIC: PAUL'S VIEWS OF THE MOSAIC LAW

▣ "the Spirit gives life" This context does not provide a hermeneutical method! This paragraph does not
relate to the historical-grammatical method of biblical hermeneutics versus the allegorical method (see
"Bible Interpretation Seminar"). It relates
primarily to the distinction between the purpose of the OT and the purpose of the NT.

Even more to the point, the role of heart-felt faith in God's resources (cf. John 6:63) versus
trusting in human resources (i.e., knowledge, works, racial standing). The key is God's love, Christ's work,
and the Spirit's enabling. Notice that both the killing of the letter and life-giving of the Spirit are both
PRESENT ACTIVE INDICATIVES.

SPECIAL TOPIC: PERSONHOOD OF THE SPIRIT

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: 2 CORINTHIANS 3:7-11

7But if the ministry of death, in letters engraved on stones, came with glory, so
that the sons of Israel could not look intently at the face of Moses because of the glory of his face, fading as it was, 8how will
the ministry of the Spirit fail to be even more with glory? 9For if the ministry of condemnation has glory, much more does the ministry
of righteousness abound in glory. 10For indeed what had glory, in this case has no glory because of the glory that surpasses it.
11For if that which fades away was with glory, much more that which remains is in glory.

3:7 "if" This is a FIRST CLASS CONDITIONAL SENTENCE which is assumed to be true from the
author's perspective or for his literary purposes.

SPECIAL TOPIC: GREEK GRAMMATICAL TERMS, VII.

▣ "the ministry of death, in letters engraved on stones" The purpose of the Mosaic law was to show sinfulness
(cf. Gal. 3:19-26). This section, 2 Cor. 3:7-18, is a rabbinical Midrash on Exod. 34:23-35. There is a threefold
use of "the veil" imagery:

- Moses

- contemporary Jews

- believers

The old covenant is written by the finger of God on tablets of stone on Mt. Sinai (cf. Exodus 19-20).
The new covenant, also written by God, is on the hearts of faithful followers (cf. Jer. 31:31-34; Ezek. 36:22-36).
The first is characterized by obedience to an external code, but the second, obedience to an internal relationship
(i.e., new heart, new mind, new spirit).

▣ "came with glory" See
SPECIAL TOPIC: GLORY (OT)

▣ "could not look intently at the face of Moses because of the glory of his face, fading as it was" This
relates to Exod. 34:30-35. There has been much discussion about this passage.

- Some think Moses veiled his face to keep the Israelites from seeing the fading glory (cf. 2 Cor. 3:7,13).

- Others, however, think Moses veiled his face because the Israelites could not stand the glory of God because of their sins

3:8 This verse is contrasting the ministry of Moses, which reflected God's glory with the ministry of the
Spirit who shares the Father's glory.

3:9 "if" This is another FIRST CLASS CONDITIONAL SENTENCE which is assumed to be true
from the author's perspective or for his literary purposes.

▣ "the ministry of condemnation" What a strong, shockingly negative way to describe the Old
Covenant. This must have been so shocking to the Jews of Paul's day, and to those modern denominations that
major on OT requirements, rituals, and festivals.

▣ "the ministry of righteousness" The OT produced condemnation for most of the children of Abraham. The NT
produces righteousness for all the children of Adam if only they will trust in God's finished work in Christ and
the wooing of the Spirit.

The OT is characterized as "had glory" (PERFECT PASSIVE INDICATIVE). It was surely
from God and reflected God (i.e., Matt. 5:17-19). However, the fuller revelation is in Christ, the glory of the NT
(PERFECT PASSIVE PARTICIPLE).

The DEFINITE ARTICLE "to" (NOMINATIVE, NEUTER, SINGULAR) is used as
a grammatical place holder for "the old covenant" (most English translations have "what"). It is characterized in this context as

- "written on tablets of stone," 2 Cor. 3:3,7

- "the letter," 2 Cor. 3:6

- "the ministry of death," 2 Cor. 3:7

- "the ministry of condemnation," 2 Cor. 3:9

This comparison of YHWH's covenants is also developed in the
book of Hebrews.

SPECIAL TOPIC: GLORY (OT)

▣ "surpasses" This is an intensified term from "over" or "beyond" and "to throw." Paul uses
it here and in 2 Cor. 9:14 (i.e., "The surpassing grace of God"). He also uses both perisseuō
and huperballō in 2 Cor. 11:23, where he compares his background and ministry with the credentials
of the false teachers. Paul speaks in 2 Corinthians with intense feelings and hyperbolic vocabulary!

SPECIAL TOPIC: PAUL'S USE OF HUPER COMPOUNDS

3:11 "if" This is another FIRST CLASS CONDITIONAL SENTENCE.

▣ "that which fades away" This is the term katargeō, which is used so often by Paul
in his Corinthian letters (cf. 1 Cor. 1:28; 2:6; 6:13; 13:8,10,11; 15:24,26; 2 Cor. 3:7,11,13,14).

SPECIAL TOPIC: NULL AND VOIC (kartageō)

▣ "that which remains is in glory" The contrast is not between that which is from God or has
God's glory, but which has the greater glory and the abiding glory. The answer is the New Covenant in Christ,
the New Age of the Spirit, and the now complete predestined eternal plan of redemption (cf. Acts 2:22-24; 3:18-21; 4:28; 13:29-41).

SPECIAL TOPIC: BOLDNESS (parrhēsia)

SPECIAL TOPIC: HUMAN SPEECH

3:13 This verse refers to verse 7, which is an allusion to Exod. 34:29-35. In the OT the reason
for Moses wearing a veil is the fear of what his glowing face might cause to the Israelites (cf. Exod. 34:30).
Paul interprets the reason so as to accentuate his depreciation of the Old Covenant. As Moses' face fades, so too,
Moses covenant!

Paul makes several comparisons between Moses' covenant and Jesus' covenant.

- the Lord of Exodus = the Spirit of Jesus

- only Moses could approach YHWH intimately versus all believers in Christ can approach Him

- Moses' glory faded versus Jesus' glory never fades

- Moses' followers cannot see Christ in the OT versus Jesus' followers through the Spirit can correctly interpret the OT in light of Christ

- Moses brought the bondage of performance versus Christ brings the freedom of grace

- the letter of the Mosaic Law brings death versus the Spirit of the New Covenant brings life, life eternal, life abundant

- Moses' covenant was unable to produce a righteous people versus Jesus' covenant does produce righteous people
(both objectively in justification and subjectively in sanctification)

3:14 "But their minds were hardened" This is an AORIST PASSIVE INDICATIVE. This Greek term comes from
the idea of "thick skinned" or "calloused" (cf. Mark 6:52; 8:17; Rom. 11:7,25). Spiritual blindness has both

- a spiritual origin

- God, by the use of the PASSIVE VOICE, cf. Isa. 6:9-10; 29:10; John 12:40; Rom. 1:24; 9:18; 2 Cor. 3:14-15

- Satan, cf. 2 Cor. 4:4

- human origin (cf. John 3:19-20; Rom. 1:19-23; 16:18)

For a good brief discussion of the theological mystery of Israel's hardening read Romans 9-11 and
Hard Sayings of the Bible from Inter Varsity Press, pp. 619-621.

The VERB "lies" in 2 Cor. 3:15 can be either PRESENT PASSIVE (i.e., #1)
or PRESENT MIDDLE (i.e., #2).

SPECIAL TOPIC: ONE CAUSALITY

SPECIAL TOPIC: SCHEMES

▣ "the same veil remains unlifted" Moses used a literal veil; this term is now used to describe
the inner blindness of contemporary Judaism (i.e., John 9). Jews were/are walking in the judgment of Deut. 29:4;
Isa. 6:9-10 and 29:10. This also relates to the Jews of our day who refuse to accept Jesus as the Messiah
(cf. 2 Cor. 3:15; 4:4).

▣ "because it is removed in Christ" Only the grace of God can remove the blindness of tradition,
self-righteousness, and sin. Religious people are as prone to spiritual blindness as non-religious people.
Fallen mankind's only hope is

- the unchanging mercy of the Father (see
SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD [OT])

- the full and finished atonement of the Son (see
SPECIAL TOPIC: ATONEMENT)

- the universal wooing/work of the Spirit (see
SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN)

Salvation is a spiritual gift and not a matter of family, tradition, intellect, or performance!

What Paul may be asserting in this context is the believer's ability through the Spirit to see the
life, teachings, and work of Jesus in the OT. Jesus Himself opened the minds of the two on the road to Emmaus
(cf. Luke 24:13-35, especially 2 Cor. 3:25-27).

3:16 "but whenever a person turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away" This could be

- a quote from Exod. 34:34. If so it relates to Moses' actions when approaching God.

- It also seems to be a universal appeal and invitation for anyone and everyone to turn to the Lord.

The term, "the Lord," here could refer contextually either to YHWH or to Jesus.
The ambiguity is probably purposeful. Notice the combined emphasis on human volitional choice and
divine action (i.e., covenant).

3:17 "Now the Lord is the Spirit" The ministry of Jesus and the Spirit are inseparably linked
(cf. John 16:7; 2 Cor. 3:17-18). The ministry of the Spirit is to magnify Jesus (cf. John 16:8-14).

In context it is possible that Paul is not commenting on the connection between Jesus and
the Spirit, but defining the word "Lord" (kurios) in 2 Cor. 3:16, which in the context of Exod. 34:34,
refers to YHWH, but Paul is using it in the sense of the REB translation, "Now the
Lord of whom this passage speaks is the Spirit." If this is accurate then the entire section is not referring to
Jesus by the term "Lord," but to the Spirit (cf. Gen. 1:2 also note Gordon D. Fee, To What End Exegesis,
pp. 218-239). This then would be the only place where Paul uses Kurios for the Spirit. It is a contrast
between the OT law code and the then unwritten gospel (i.e., written versus living).

SPECIAL TOPIC: Lord (adon and kurios)

▣ "there is liberty" This refers to freedom from spiritual blindness, self-righteousness,
tradition, and legalism caused by a personal faith relationship with Jesus Christ (cf. John 8:32,36; Rom. 14: 1 Cor. 8;
10:23ff; Gal. 5:1,13).

One of my favorite commentators, F. F. Bruce, in his book, Paul: Apostle of the Heart Set Free, says

"Paul certainly knew the love of Christ to be the all-compelling power in life.
Where love is the compelling power, there is no sense of strain or conflict or bondage in doing
what is right: the man or woman who is compelled by Jesus' love and empowered by his Spirit does
the will of God from the heart. For (as Paul could say from experience) 'where the Spirit of
the Lord is, there the heart is free'" (p. 21).

Believers must be careful with freedom/liberty. Self-asserting freedom can become
a prideful, self-centered weapon. It is freedom "from," not freedom "to" (cf. Gal. 5:1,13-26). We
are free in Christ from the terrible, recurrent pull of self and sin! We are now free to be like Him!

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHRISTIAN FREEDOM vs.
CHRISTIAN RESPONSIBILITY

3:18 "with unveiled face" This is a PERFECT PASSIVE PARTICIPLE implying a permanent
unveiling. Also note the inclusive "we all" referring to the believers in the confused and factious
Corinthian church.

▣ "beholding as in a mirror the glory of the Lord" The gospel has fully revealed both YHWH and
Jesus of Nazareth (cf. 2 Cor. 4:6) as well as our own sinfulness. As we respond in repentance and faith the revelation changes us into
His image. This same imagery is found in 2 Cor. 4:4. These Corinthian Christians had clearly seen YHWH
in Christ through the gospel.

The term "beholding" is a rare term. The Greek-English Lexicon of the New Testament and
Other Early Christian Literature by Bauer, Arndt, Gingrich and Danker lists the possible uses based
on the voice (p. 424).

- ACTIVE, produce a reflection

- PASSIVE, what is seen in a mirror

- MIDDLE, look at oneself in a mirror

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE GOSPEL

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE KERYGMA OF THE EARLY CHURCH

▣ "are being transformed" This is a PREENT PASSIVE INDICATIVE. All of the VERBALS
in this context are PASSIVE VOICE, implying the Father's or the Spirit's activity on our behalf, transforming believers into
Christ's likeness (cf. Rom. 8:28-29; 2 Cor. 7:1; Gal. 4:19; Eph. 1:4; 4:13; 1 Thess. 3:13; 4:3,7; 5:23; 1 Pet. 1:15; also note "transformed" in
Rom. 12:2; Phil. 3:21). This same VERB is used of the Transfiguration (cf. Matt. 17:2; Mark 9:2).
We get the English word metamorphosis from this Greek term.

▣ "into the same image" Jesus is the image of God (cf. 2 Cor. 4:4; John 1:14-18; 14:9; Col. 1:15;
Heb. 1:3). Humans were created in the image of God (cf. Gen. 1:26-27; see exegetical notes online). Believers are in the image of Christ
(cf. Rom. 8:29-30). Christlikeness is God's primary goal for all believers (see list of texts above).

Notice the number of ways Paul uses "image" to describe Jesus.

- "the image of His Son," Rom. 8:29

- "the image of the heavenly," 1 Cor. 15:49

- "glory of the Lord. . .into the same image from glory to glory," 2 Cor. 3:18

- "the image of God," 2 Cor. 4:4

- "the image of the invisible God," Col. 1:15

Also note similar characterizations

- "only begotten of the Father," John 1:18

- "he existed in the form of God," Phil. 2:6

- "He is. . .the exact representation of His nature," Heb. 1:3

▣ "from glory to glory" There are stages in God's plan of restoration and renewal. Believers
are in a process that leads to Christlikeness (cf. 1 John 3:2).

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are
responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You,
the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this
section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

- Describe the difference between the Old Covenant and the New Covenant?

- Why is the OT said to be death? Does this mean the OT is evil?

- What is the relationship between the OT and the NT?

- Does this passage speak of the Holy Spirit or the spiritual realm?

- What is the metaphor of "the veil" trying to communicate to modern day Christians?
